title: Sliding Window Maximum
description:
# Sliding Window Maximum

You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. A window of exactly `k` consecutive elements moves from the left side of the array to the right side, one position at a time.

Return an array where the i-th value is the maximum element inside the window `nums[i..i + k - 1]`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3
**Output:** [3,3,5,5,6,7]
**Explanation:** The six windows are [1,3,-1], [3,-1,-3], [-1,-3,5], [-3,5,3], [5,3,6], and [3,6,7]. Their maximum values are [3,3,5,5,6,7].

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1], k = 1
**Output:** [1]
**Explanation:** The only window contains the only element.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= nums.length <= 10^5`
*   `-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4`
*   `1 <= k <= nums.length`

tests.description: Canonical mixed increasing and decreasing windows
Later value becomes the maximum after the old maximum leaves
Repeated maxima with ties across windows
Negative values with a late improving maximum

solutions.name: Monotonic Deque - Optimal
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store indices in a deque. The values at those indices are kept in decreasing order, so the front index is always the maximum candidate for the current window. Before inserting a new index, remove expired indices from the front and remove dominated smaller or equal values from the back.

## Key Insight

An older value that is no larger than the new value can never be the maximum of a future window while the new value is still inside the window. Keeping indices instead of values is what lets the algorithm expire elements exactly when they leave the window.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(k)

solutions.name: Max Heap with Lazy Removal
solutions.description:
## Approach

Push each pair `(value, index)` into a max heap as the right edge advances. Before reading the maximum for a full window, repeatedly remove heap entries whose stored index is no longer inside the window.

## Key Insight

The heap may contain stale entries, but a stale entry only matters when it reaches the top. Lazy removal keeps the implementation simple and shows a general priority-queue pattern for window problems, at the cost of logarithmic operations.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Block Decomposition Left and Right Max
solutions.description:
## Approach

Split the array into blocks of length `k`. Precompute `leftMax[i]`, the maximum from the start of the block through `i`, and `rightMax[i]`, the maximum from `i` through the end of the block. A window maximum is then `max(rightMax[start], leftMax[end])`.

## Key Insight

Every fixed-length window crosses at most one block boundary. The left part of the window is answered by a suffix maximum and the right part by a prefix maximum, so the query becomes constant time after preprocessing.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: TreeMap Multiset Window
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain the current window as a multiset backed by a `TreeMap` from value to count. Insert the entering value, remove one copy of the leaving value once the window is too large, and read `lastKey()` as the maximum after each full window.

## Key Insight

A balanced multiset is a direct baseline for sliding window extrema. It is slower than the monotonic deque but easier to reason about when equal values must be counted correctly, because removing one occurrence does not remove all equal maxima.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log k)
- Space Complexity: O(k)
